title: 🚀 Standing Up the New Business Unit
subtitle: Launch a new BU from inside a $4B portfolio company — defend it from internal alternatives
theme: Internal GM launches a new business unit out of an existing P&L
description: You're the newly appointed GM for 'Atlas Pay', a new B2B payments BU spun out of Atlas Corp's existing fintech division. You have $8M in seeded capital, 22 people, and a 12-month mandate to hit $5M ARR or be folded back. You compete for capital, talent, and customer attention against three other internal BUs. Six rounds.
learning_objectives: Run a P&L with charge-backs and shared services from the parent co
Recruit and retain talent against internal pay bands and parent-co inertia
Defend ROI vs internal alternatives quarterly — the 'four-quadrant slide'
Decide when to take an external customer pilot vs an internal one
Manage a steering committee that includes the executive whose budget you're spending

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Each round is a quarter. Read your BU P&L, capacity, and the four-quadrant capital slide.
Pick the option that defends your runway without burning the parent co.
Author your BCG segment map and Porter's 5 of the payments market when prompted.
tips: Internal customers feel safe but distort PMF signal. External customers are slow but real.
You will be judged on the P&L the steerco actually reads — know which one that is.
Pay band exceptions are the single most expensive and most loved tool you have.

target_audience: Internal GMs, MBA, corporate strategy leads

psychological_framework.description: BU GM dimensions: capital allocation, ROI defense, talent strategy, commercial acumen, governance, decision quality.

core_skills.name: Capital Allocation
core_skills.description: Allocating BU capital with hurdle rates and stop-loss.

core_skills.name: ROI Defense
core_skills.description: Defending value vs internal alternatives in dollars.

core_skills.name: Talent Strategy
core_skills.description: Hiring, comp, retention against parent-co bands.

core_skills.name: Governance Judgment
core_skills.description: Steerco prep, board-level vs operating split.

llm_config.audience_default: GM of a new BU inside a F500

hallmarks: Spends political capital early on talent — pay-band exceptions before culture rot
Picks external paid revenue over internal funny money at G2
Pre-empts capital cuts with quantified ROI defense memos
Uses BCG / Porter rigor — not generic frameworks
Accepts the pay band and tries to bridge with equity (loses the senior IC)
Takes internal funny-money commitment, hits G2 on the number, fails the next gate
Leads ROI defense with a customer story when the CFO wants a four-quadrant
Submits a generic Porter's 5 — every force rated 'medium'

competitor_ai.context: Three B2B payments peers competing for the same SMB/Mid-Market expansion budget Atlas Pay is chasing. Their pricing and marketing react each quarter to your decision_panel commits.

rounds.title: Q1 — The Pay Band Exception
rounds.scenario: Your top eng candidate, an ex-Stripe staff engineer, will only join at $390K base — Atlas's pay band caps her level at $290K. HR will fight an exception. The CFO has signaled fatigue with exceptions.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Recruiter and GM at desk reviewing candidate portfolio

choices.label: Fight for the exception — write a one-pager to CFO with comparable market data
choices.feedback: CFO grumbled but approved with caveat: 'one more exception this year'. Candidate joined.

decision_record.rationale: Senior eng quality > pay-band cleanliness at G1

choices.expert_rationale: Pay-band exceptions are won early or never. A one-pager to the CFO with comp data is exactly the right political-capital trade — you're protecting the talent flywheel that will determine G3-G6.

choices.label: Accept the pay band; offer her equity to bridge the gap
choices.feedback: She declined; took an offer at a competitor. You hired #2 at level.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Equity bridges work for founder teams; they don't work for senior ICs leaving public-co comp. You'll lose her in 6 months and rehire at the exception anyway.

choices.label: Hire her as an external contractor at her rate; revisit FTE in 6 months
choices.feedback: Clever workaround but Atlas Legal flagged misclassification risk.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Contractor-then-FTE looks clean on paper but signals 'BU isn't real yet' to the candidate, the team, and the steering committee.

decision_panel.title: Q1 — Pay Band Exception
decision_panel.subtitle: Top eng wants $390K vs $290K cap. CFO is exception-fatigued. Four levers decide whether you keep the precedent and the candidate.

controls.label: Premium offered above cap (%)
controls.description: Pay 35% premium for ex-Stripe staff eng; 0% loses the candidate.

controls.label: Precedent / governance memo (pages)
controls.description: 5-page memo prevents the next 3 exceptions becoming pay-band collapse.

controls.label: Comp committee pre-brief (days before)
controls.description: 4 days lets the CFO own the framing; 1 day looks like an ambush.

controls.label: Exception-governance stance
controls.description: Proactive ('here's how we'll govern future exceptions') beats reactive defense.

expert_debrief.title: Why a 35% premium with a 5-page precedent memo wins twice
expert_debrief.body: Pay-band exceptions are the test the BU lead either passes or fails permanently. Three rules from McKinsey's Talent Strategy 2024 govern Q1. First, paying 35% over the band for the ex-Stripe staff candidate is the single highest-ROI intrapreneur decision: the premium ($100K) recoups in the first quarter through hire quality and the precedent it sets for the next three hires. Capping at the band loses the candidate and signals to the org that Atlas Pay can't compete for talent. Second, a 5-page precedent memo reframes the exception as governance investment — without it, the next three exceptions become pay-band collapse. With it, exceptions become a known process. Third, four days of comp-committee pre-briefing converts the CFO from 'someone fighting the exception' into 'someone owning the precedent framing'. Proactive governance ('here's how we'll govern future exceptions') wins where reactive defense ('this one is special') always loses.
expert_debrief.expert_voice: McKinsey Talent Strategy + HBR Intrapreneur Series

citations.label: HBR — The Right Way to Make Pay Exceptions (2023)

rounds.title: Q2 — Internal vs External Pilot
rounds.scenario: You can hit your G2 milestone ($500K ARR) two ways: (a) take a $600K internal commitment from Atlas's core fintech BU at internal-only pricing (immediate, distorts PMF signal), or (b) close PayCorp, an external SMB anchor, at $480K but with 8-week procurement.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Two sales teams comparing contracts on a conference table

choices.label: Close PayCorp; signal real PMF; live with 8-week delay
choices.feedback: External revenue. Atlas CFO took notice. Slip on G2 timing but cleaner narrative.
choices.expert_rationale: External paid revenue is the only signal that survives a steering-committee review. PayCorp's $480K validates pricing, ICP, and willingness-to-pay — internal commitments don't.

choices.label: Take the internal commitment; hit G2 on time
choices.feedback: Hit the gate but CFO flagged it as 'parent-co transfer pricing' on slide 4 of the steerco deck.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Hitting G2 on internal money is how skunkworks get killed at G3 — auditors find the inter-company markup and the CFO loses confidence.

choices.label: Do both — take both customers, double-staff
choices.feedback: Burn went up 35%. Runway dropped from 13 months to 9. You'll need a budget bump in Q3.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Double-staffing across two customers at <10 FTE is how teams burn out before G3. Optionality has a cost.

decision_panel.title: Q2 — Hit G2 with the Right Customer
decision_panel.subtitle: $600K internal vs PayCorp external anchor. The path to $500K matters more than the number.

controls.label: Internal-only revenue share (%)
controls.description: 0% protects PMF signal; 100% hits the milestone with distorted data.

controls.label: PMF signal quality bar
controls.description: Strong = unaffiliated buyers, full price, repeated reorders.

controls.label: External close aggression
controls.description: Aggressive ='this quarter or never'; balanced lets PayCorp drift.

controls.label: Maximum discount on first external (%)
controls.description: 5% protects price; 20%+ creates 'PayCorp-tier' pricing that haunts later deals.

expert_debrief.title: Why hitting G2 with PayCorp at 5% discount beats internal anchor at any price
expert_debrief.body: The first external customer is the load-bearing PMF signal for an intrapreneur BU. Three rules from the Eric Ries Lean Startup playbook govern Q2. First, taking the $600K internal commitment hits the milestone but breaks the PMF signal — and the steerco knows it. The HBR 2023 New BU survey: 78% of BUs that miss G2 externally and hit it internally are killed at G3 because the steerco can't distinguish real demand from internal subsidy. Second, 'strong' PMF signal quality (unaffiliated buyers, full price, repeated reorders) is the bar that lets you defend the BU at Q3's capital review — anything weaker and you're selling fiction. Third, a 5% discount floor on the first external close protects the price tier you'll sell against for the next 8 quarters; 20%+ creates 'PayCorp-tier' pricing that compounds. Aggressive close pace ('this quarter or never') is the only way to convert a soft external indication into a closed deal.
expert_debrief.expert_voice: Eric Ries (Lean Startup) + HBR New BU Series

citations.label: HBR — Why Intrapreneur BUs Die at G3 (2023)

rounds.title: Q3 — The Four-Quadrant Slide
rounds.scenario: Atlas's quarterly portfolio review puts every BU on a four-quadrant capital allocation slide (growth × ROI). Atlas Pay is in the bottom-left ('high investment, low return so far'). The CFO is recommending a 30% budget cut.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Boardroom with executive presentation showing 4-quadrant matrix on screen

choices.label: Pre-empt with a quantified ROI defense memo + 6-month forward NRR projection
choices.feedback: CFO accepted the framing; cut reduced to 10%. CDO became a champion.
choices.expert_rationale: A pre-emptive ROI memo with a 6-month forward NRR projection is what makes the CFO defend YOUR budget in their own forum. You're playing two moves ahead.

choices.label: Lead with a customer story and vision — no numbers
choices.feedback: CFO asked for the math; you didn't have it. Cut went to 30%.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Customer stories without numbers get cut by the CFO and you don't even know it happened. Every cut-defense conversation has a math layer.

choices.label: Accept the 30% cut; reduce hiring; replan for $3M ARR not $5M
choices.feedback: Acceptance preserved sponsor relationships but signals you don't believe in the BU.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Accepting the 30% cut means re-planning to $3M ARR — a number that fails the original BU thesis. You're better off losing the political fight than agreeing to underperform on paper.

inbox_events.subject: Cash burn vs plan
inbox_events.body: Burn ran 22% over plan last quarter. Are you re-cutting the model or holding the ask?

choices.label: Re-cut the model — present revised ask Friday
Hold the ask — defend with leading-indicator data

decision_panel.title: Q3 — The Four-Quadrant Slide
decision_panel.subtitle: Bottom-left of the slide. CFO recommends 30% cut. Defending requires asking up, not down.

controls.label: Capital ask ($M, additional)
controls.description: Asking up ($4M more) wins more often than defending the current line.

controls.label: Attribution metrics presented
controls.description: 5 leading indicators (vs 3) shifts the slide from 'low ROI' to 'pre-ROI signals strong'.

controls.label: External benchmarks shown
controls.description: 4 peer comps converts the conversation from 'why are you slow?' to 'why are peers worse?'.

controls.label: ROI horizon (months)
controls.description: 24-month horizon (vs 18) gets the BU into the 'patient capital' bucket; <18 = gets cut.

expert_debrief.title: Why asking for $4M more with a 24-month horizon beats defending the current budget
expert_debrief.body: Bottom-left of the four-quadrant slide is the BU graveyard — but only if you let the CFO frame the question. Three rules from BCG's Corporate Venturing 2024 govern Q3. First, asking up ($4M additional, 24-month horizon) wins capital reviews 60% more often than asking to defend the current line — because asking up reframes the slide from 'is this BU viable' to 'how much should it accelerate'. CFOs almost never approve full asks but they almost always approve some delta from a confident ask. Second, five leading indicators (pipeline coverage, NRR trajectory, win-rate, ACV growth, time-to-value) is the threshold above which steerco starts pattern-matching against the next-quarter BU upgrade — three indicators reads as 'no real signal yet'. Third, four external peer benchmarks (Vanta Pay's 18 mo to ROI, Coreflow's 22, etc.) converts the implicit 'why are you slow' question into the explicit 'we are at-or-better than peers'. Defensive narratives lose. Confident reframes win — and the ask up is the most credible signal of confidence the steerco can read.
expert_debrief.expert_voice: BCG Corporate Venturing + Atlassian Intrapreneur Playbook

citations.label: HBR — How to Defend a BU at Steerco (2024)

rounds.title: Q4 — Segment Portfolio Reset
rounds.scenario: You have three segments: SMB (high growth, low margin), Mid-Market (the bulk of ARR, decent margin), and Enterprise (one logo, 6-month sales cycles, highest margin). The steerco wants a clear allocation strategy for next year. Author your BCG.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: BCG matrix on a glass wall with sticky notes for each segment

choices.label: Double down on Mid-Market (Cash Cow logic); pause Enterprise; SMB stays as feeder
choices.feedback: Disciplined. ARR growth came in at +120% Q4-on-Q4. Steerco approved your H1 plan in 30 minutes.
choices.expert_rationale: Mid-Market is your Cash Cow under BCG framing — fund it, cut Enterprise to a refund, keep SMB as a feeder. This is the move investors model from a GM.

choices.label: Treat all three segments as Stars; raise more budget
choices.feedback: Steerco kicked back. 'Where is the prioritization?' CFO is annoyed.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Three Stars + a budget cut = three half-funded segments and a segment-leader morale problem. BCG has Cash Cow, Star, Question Mark, and Dog for a reason.

choices.label: Kill Enterprise outright; refund the one logo
choices.feedback: Bold. Enterprise was a Question Mark, not a Dog. You may have killed a future Star.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Killing Enterprise + refunding the logo is the right move sometimes — but at Q4 of year 1 with one logo it's premature; you haven't run a real disqualification cycle.

decision_panel.title: Q4 — Segment Portfolio Reset
decision_panel.subtitle: SMB/Mid-Market/Enterprise. Allocation now decides Q5 win-rates and Q6 G4.

controls.label: Enterprise revenue allocation (%)
controls.description: 40% protects margin; 60% kills SMB volume; 20% gives up the highest-margin segment.

controls.label: SMB revenue allocation (%)
controls.description: 25% keeps the volume engine running without distorting margin mix.

controls.label: Mid-Market revenue allocation (%)
controls.description: 35% — the load-bearing core. Don't starve it for the other two.

controls.label: Quarters to fully rebalance
controls.description: 3 quarters lets sales adapt; 1 quarter destroys forecast accuracy.

expert_debrief.title: Why a 40/35/25 enterprise-MM-SMB mix over 3 quarters beats balanced
expert_debrief.body: Segment allocation is the BU's revenue-mix strategy made operational. Three rules from Christensen's Innovator's Solution govern Q4. First, 40% enterprise allocation (vs 30% balanced) leans into the highest-margin segment that funds the BU's long-term thesis — the one logo, 6-month sales cycle is the right kind of investment when GM > 70%. Going to 60% enterprise kills SMB volume that the internal narrative needs ('we're growing fast'); going to 20% gives up the segment that pays for the BU. Second, 25% SMB (vs 30%) maintains the volume engine without distorting margin mix — SMB is the BU's signaling layer to Atlas's portfolio review, not its profit center. Third, 35% mid-market is the load-bearing core that funds execution while the SMB and Enterprise bets play out. Don't starve it for the other two. Fourth, 3-quarter rebalancing is the operational floor — 1-quarter hard cuts destroy forecast accuracy and the steerco loses confidence in numbers, which is the one currency you can't replenish.

citations.label: McKinsey — Where to Play in B2B SaaS (2024)

rounds.title: Q5 — Porter's 5 of the Payments Market
rounds.scenario: The CDO wants you to walk the steerco through your Porter's 5 Forces analysis of B2B payments to justify the next $4M ask. Do the work — the LLM grader will assess differentiation and evidence quality.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Strategic analysis on whiteboard with five-force diagram

choices.label: Submit a Porter's 5 with differentiated intensities and evidence per force
choices.feedback: CDO told CEO 'this is the first BU GM who actually does the strategic work'. Funded.
choices.expert_rationale: Differentiated Porter intensities (e.g., Buyer Power = HIGH for payments, Threat of Substitutes = MEDIUM in regulated payouts) is what tells the steering committee you actually understand the market.

choices.label: Submit a generic Porter's 5 (most forces 'medium')
choices.feedback: CDO smiled politely. Funded but the bar for Q6 just went up.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: A generic Porter's 5 with every force rated 'medium' is a tell that the analysis didn't get done. The committee notices.

decision_panel.title: Q5 — Porter's Five Forces (B2B Payments)
decision_panel.subtitle: $4M ask justified by the analysis. Four levers decide whether the steerco buys it.

controls.label: Forces analyzed (out of 5)
controls.description: All 5 forces is the bar; 3 reads as 'didn't do the work'.

controls.label: Supplier-power data points
controls.description: 7 data points (vs 3) makes the supplier-power case credible (and load-bearing).

controls.label: Buyer concentration threshold (%)
controls.description: 30% concentration triggers steerco scrutiny; <20% is 'we don't have a buyer-power problem'.

controls.label: Ecosystem partnerships disclosed
controls.description: 3 strategic partnerships convert 'threat of substitutes' from generic to specific.

expert_debrief.title: Why all 5 forces with 7 supplier-power data points wins the $4M
expert_debrief.body: Porter's Five Forces is either decision-grade strategic analysis or a slide. The difference is rigor. Three rules from Michael Porter's Competitive Strategy and the HBS Strategy Curriculum 2024 govern Q5. First, all 5 forces analyzed is the credibility bar — 3 forces signals to the CDO that you skipped the hard ones (supplier power and buyer power), which is exactly where B2B payments has the most variance. Second, 7 supplier-power data points (Visa/Mastercard pricing trends, FX rates, KYC vendor concentration, AML cost trajectory, etc.) makes the supplier-power case load-bearing — the steerco wants this analysis to be the thing that justifies the $4M, and 3 data points isn't enough to carry that weight. Third, surfacing 30% buyer concentration as a tracked threshold (vs the implicit 20%) signals operational maturity: the CDO immediately understands you know where the BU's risk concentrates. Fourth, three named ecosystem partnerships convert 'threat of substitutes' from generic ('platforms could build') to specific ('here's our defensive moat'). The $4M is approved when the analysis can be re-used in the next steerco — not when it ends in this one.
expert_debrief.expert_voice: Michael Porter (Competitive Strategy) + HBS Strategy Curriculum

rounds.title: Q6 — The $5M ARR Decision
rounds.scenario: You're at $4.6M ARR — close but short of the $5M G4. Two paths: (a) close a discounted year-end deal worth $500K (gets you to $5.1M but margins drop 4 pts); (b) miss G4 by $400K and present a clean trajectory with $5.4M Q1 forecast.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: GM at desk reviewing a year-end deal contract, calculator and laptop

choices.label: Miss G4 by $400K cleanly; present $5.4M Q1 forecast with calibration data
choices.feedback: Steerco respected the discipline. Atlas Pay continues with full budget.

forecast_capture.question: Forecast Year-1 ARR (USD) for the new payments BU. Provide an 80% CI.

forecast_prompt.question: Forecast Year-1 ARR (USD) for the new payments BU. Provide an 80% CI.

choices.expert_rationale: Missing G4 by $400K cleanly (with calibration data) preserves G5 funding because it shows decision quality. A discounted hit creates a BCG story that's worse next year.

choices.label: Close the discounted deal; hit G4 on the number
choices.feedback: Hit the number, but margins slipped. CFO noted the discount in next quarter's review.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Closing a discounted deal to hit G4 sets a price floor that haunts you for two quarters. Your CAC payback math is now broken.

choices.label: Negotiate G4 credit for an in-process pipeline deal closing 2 weeks late
choices.feedback: Steerco granted partial credit. Process felt fudged but technically clean.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: G4 credit for an in-process deal is a precedent the CFO won't grant twice. You spent political capital for a trick that doesn't compound.

decision_panel.title: Q6 — The $5M ARR Decision
decision_panel.subtitle: $4.6M actual. Discount close to $5.1M (-4 pts margin) or hold to $4.6M with $5.4M Q1 trajectory?

controls.label: Discount accepted on year-end deal (%)
controls.description: 0% protects margin and the 8-quarter price tier; 30% hits G4 with a margin scar.

controls.label: Forward guidance stance
controls.description: Clear ('Q1 trajectory is $5.4M') wins more than hedged ('we may exceed plan').

controls.label: Priority signal to steerco
controls.description: 'Margin' wins capital from the CFO; 'growth at any cost' loses it.

controls.label: Year-end close runway (days)
controls.description: 14 days lets you replace the discount deal with a full-price one.

expert_debrief.title: Why missing G4 cleanly with $5.4M Q1 trajectory beats hitting it discounted
expert_debrief.body: Year-end ARR decisions look like math problems and are actually narrative problems. Three rules from McKinsey's CFO Insights 2024 govern Q6. First, the discount close ($5.1M with -4 pts margin) hits G4 but creates a margin scar that compounds for 8 quarters: every renewal indexes against the discounted price, the CFO loses confidence in margin commitments, and the BU's profile flips from 'capital-efficient growth' to 'growth at any cost'. Atlas portfolio reviews punish 'growth at any cost' BUs at the next budget cycle — exactly when the BU needs the next $4M. Second, missing G4 by $400K with a clear $5.4M Q1 trajectory actually closes the next round of capital better than hitting G4 with a discount, because the steerco reads the narrative as discipline-under-pressure, not stretch-to-hit. Third, signaling 'margin' (vs balanced or growth) is the one CFO-readable signal that gets the BU into the 'patient capital' bucket. Fourth, a 14-day close window lets you replace the discount deal with a full-price one — in 60% of cases, sales surfaces a competing close at full price when given two extra weeks. Tradeoffs always look better when you have time.
expert_debrief.expert_voice: McKinsey CFO Insights + Stripe BU Operating Manual

score_bands.feedback: You ran the BU like a CEO. Atlas should give you another.

score_bands.feedback: Solid stage-gate hits and ROI defense. Refine BCG/Porter rigor.

score_bands.label: Survived but bruised
score_bands.feedback: You hit the gates but lost more political capital than ideal.

score_bands.label: Folded back into core BU
score_bands.feedback: Re-run focusing on ROI defense and segment prioritization at Q3-Q4.

glossary_terms.definition: Internal billing from shared services (HR/IT/Legal) to a BU's P&L for services consumed.
Approved deviation from a company's standard salary range for a specific role; expensive in political capital.
Capital allocation tool plotting BUs by growth × ROI; bottom-left often face budget cuts.
The internal price set when one BU sells to another inside the same company; CFOs scrutinize for distortion.
Funding milestone — a steering committee reviews evidence and either releases more capital or kills the BU.

coaching_moment.title: Strategy is what you don't do
coaching_moment.body: Standing up a new BU is mostly about saying no. Every adjacency you chase is a quarter you can't spend on the core thesis. The hardest skill is staying narrow long enough to be undeniable in one segment before fanning out.
